BBC, 25 Nov 2026 06:21 GMT

MPs demand meeting with water chief over outages

Four Norfolk MPs want answers after several areas of the county were left without supplies

Double hot and cold tap over a bath. Water trickles from it. A shower is behind the bath in the background.

Labour MPs have written to Anglian Water demanding an urgent meeting following what they described as \"a week of major water supply failures\" across Norfolk.

Ben Goldsborough of South Norfolk, Terry Jermy of South West Norfolk, Alice Macdonald of Norwich North and Clive Lewis of Norwich South have called for a meeting in Westminster with chief executive Mark Thurston.

In their letter, they cited outages from 16 November, claiming \"thousands of households\" were left without water.

The company has apologised, saying two events on 17 and 20 November had halted supplies or caused a loss of pressure, but that it was \"inaccurate\" to say customers were left without water for a prolonged period.

The MPs said the disruption initially affected Costessey and the villages of Easton  and Marlingford before escalating into a major outage across Norwich on Friday, also affecting nearby Cringleford and Keswick.

An Anglian Water spokesman said: \"Our teams responded to two separate incidents. One was caused by damage to one of our water mains by a third party, while the other was the result of a pumping issue.

\"In both cases, our teams acted quickly to rezone the network and redirect supplies to customers which were restored within two hours while repairs and further work on the network continued.

\"We understand that any loss of water supply or reduced water pressure is frustrating for customers and we apologise to those customers affected in Norfolk last week.\"

Mark Thurston has been asked to meet Norfolk MPs

In their letter, the MPs said they were \"demanding a full explanation of the equipment failures, details of the company's investment and maintenance programme, assurances about compensation for affected households and a clear plan to prevent further outages\".

Goldsborough told the BBC that in Stoke Holy Cross, near Norwich, a damaged Victorian pipe had been waiting two years to be fixed.

\"The thing with Norfolk is a lot of our infrastructure is getting on a bit nowadays. And it's more tricky to do. It takes longer to do and it costs more money,\" he said.

\"We all know in our villages that when they fix a metre of pipe with brand new plastics, the next metre along, which is the old Victorian pipe, then bursts immediately because the pressure is too high.

\"We're seeing this piecemeal approach by Anglian Water and it's just not on for our constituents.\"

The MPs also demanded an explanation of \"a reported £500,000 retention payment\" to Thurston, adding it sent \"an appalling message\" to customers.

In response, an Anglian Water spokesman explained that retention payments were made to retain high-calibre staff and funded by a different company within the group.

He said it was shareholders who decided who to fund and over what period.

\"These arrangements do not replace bonuses and are not paid for by Anglian Water Services or customers,\" he added.

Thurston's bonus was withheld after a pollution incident killed fish in Essex in August

Thurston was denied his annual bonus of £1.05m last month after thousands of tonnes of raw sewage ended up in the River Mardyke in Grays, Essex.

Anglian Water has also recently been criticised for its environmental impact and  told it \"requires improvement\" for the fifth year in a row.

British people, particularly teens and young adults, are having less or no sex compared to past generations, but lots are watching porn and sexting, a major study suggests.

It is the first time The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles' (Natsal) research into general public sex lives has asked about online behaviours.

The latest results were published in The Lancet and were based on a survey of 6,700 people aged 16–59 who were selected at random across Britain.

Energy bills will rise by 26% for millions of households in January, the highest rate in nearly four years, after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

Isaac, a student at Durham University, said he had no choice but to keep the heating in his student house on 'constantly' due to poor insulation, and he was not looking forward to the price increase.

In the Autumn budget, the government announced a one-off payment of £100 for households in council bands A to D, 'half a weekly shop' according to Isaac.
